title_original: 14th review – Ava DuVernay takes on a bully president and his viper’s-nest court of Maga sycophants
excerpt_original: DuVernay’s follow-up to her dissection of the 13th Amendment to the US constitution is a vehement and exhilarating defence of democracy Ava DuVernay’s previous documentary 13th , energised by the Black Lives Matter movement, was a brilliant polemic about the Thirteenth Amendment…

blocks.text: A va DuVernay’s previous documentary 13th , energised by the Black Lives Matter movement, was a brilliant polemic about the Thirteenth Amendment to the US constitution , which she argued perpetuated a link between slavery and prison for African American men. Ten years later, and after an almost continuous decade of Trumpism, DuVernay has made a follow-up film about the Fourteenth Amendment , and she has evidently arrived at a rather different attitude to the constitution and its authors’ intentions and good faith. Now she sees the enemy as Maga and the constitution as something that must be defended against a tinpot bully president and his viper’s-nest court of sycophants.

links.text: Thirteenth Amendment to the US constitution

blocks.text: The shift in view is not acknowledged, but the overall effect is similar. Utilising a gallery of very smart talking-head interviewees, including conservative Republicans, DuVernay has mounted a vehement and exhilarating defence of what might be called the second American Enlightenment, created by the 13th, 14th and 15th “reconstruction” amendments, drawn up between 1865 and 1870 after the American civil war. The 14th specifically established birthright citizenship, due process and equal rights for all races under the law, and furthermore barred insurrectionists from holding public office, all of which Trump appears casually intent on vandalising, airily amnesiac about his oath to uphold the constitution.

As before, DuVernay does a really good job of schooling the audience in how all this stems from the historical trauma of the civil war, at the end of which the south was defeated – less like Germany in 1945, more like Germany in 1918. She shows that in the decades that followed, the secessionists had to be appeased and placated in the interests of calm coexistence: the statues of Robert E Lee and other standard-bearers of the “Lost Cause” which proliferated, some as late as the 1940s and 50s, were tolerated as a kind of cultural identity expression, and the Confederate flag transformed from an icon of slavery into a quaint, picturesque style accessory for T-shirts, hubcaps and electric guitars.

This all came out of a backlash that followed the war and DuVernay elegantly shows that Maga is an analogous, microcosmic backlash to the unthinkable disgrace of having had a Black president from 2009 to 2017. Only this time, the United States is actually coming very close to smashing up constitutional rights that somehow stayed in place, at least theoretically, throughout the Jim Crow era. At all events, for a British audience, the idea of a written constitution seems like a utopian luxury.
